patient.chief_complaint: Persistent left shoulder stiffness and left arm not swinging when walking, referred from orthopedic surgery for neurological evaluation after inadequate response to adhesive capsulitis treatment
patient.history_present_illness:
Mr. Kim is a 73-year-old right-handed Korean-American retired accountant who is referred to neurology by his orthopedic surgeon for persistent left shoulder stiffness and left arm movement difficulty that has not responded adequately to treatment for adhesive capsulitis over the past 18 months. He is accompanied by his adult son, who provides additional history.

Approximately two years ago, the patient and his family noticed that he no longer swung his left arm when walking. He and his wife attributed this initially to getting older. About 18 months ago he began experiencing left shoulder aching and stiffness with restricted range of motion. He was evaluated by orthopedic surgery, who diagnosed left-shoulder adhesive capsulitis based on restricted passive and active range of motion. Plain films showed no fracture; ultrasound showed no rotator cuff tear. He received two corticosteroid injections into the left glenohumeral joint and completed 12 weeks of physical therapy. His shoulder range of motion improved only marginally. A cervical spine MRI ordered at that time demonstrated C5-C6 spondylosis with mild foraminal narrowing, which the spine team considered unlikely to account for the shoulder-predominant picture. The orthopedic surgeon noted on his most recent visit that the shoulder stiffness had a different quality than typical frozen shoulder — the arm just did not move naturally — and has now referred him to neurology.

On direct neurological questioning today, the patient and his son report that over the past 12 to 15 months the patient's left hand has developed an intermittent trembling at rest, which stops when he reaches for something and returns when his hand is in his lap. He has noticed increasing difficulty with fine motor tasks on the left: buttoning shirts is labored, and his handwriting has become smaller. His son notes that his father appears to move more slowly in general, takes longer to rise from chairs, and shuffles more than before. The patient reports diminished sense of smell over the past two years, which he had not previously mentioned to any physician. He also reports worsening constipation and occasional lightheadedness when standing quickly. His wife has told him that he sometimes acts out his dreams at night — she has been kicked twice. He denies hallucinations, significant cognitive decline beyond mild word-finding difficulty, and denies any falls to date.

He takes no medications known to cause parkinsonism. He has never taken antipsychotics, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, or promethazine.

results.title: Shoulder pain and reduced arm swing as early manifestations of Parkinson's disease
results.authors: Tinazzi M, Recchia S, Simonetto S et al.
results.key_finding: Shoulder pain and stiffness are among the most common initial complaints in patients subsequently diagnosed with Parkinson's disease. Unilateral shoulder stiffness refractory to orthopedic management should prompt neurological evaluation when accompanied by ipsilateral arm-swing reduction.

results.title: MDS clinical diagnostic criteria for Parkinson's disease
results.authors: Postuma RB, Berg D, Stern M et al.
results.key_finding: Clinically established PD requires bradykinesia plus at least one of rest tremor or rigidity; two or more supportive criteria (including clear and dramatic beneficial response to levodopa and rest tremor of a limb); and absence of absolute exclusion criteria and red flags. [Postuma_2015]

results.title: Parkinson's disease is overdiagnosed clinically at baseline in diagnostically uncertain cases: a 3-year EU multicentre study with repeat (123I)FP-CIT SPECT
results.authors: Marshall VL, Patterson J, Hadley DM et al.
results.key_finding: Dopamine transporter SPECT (DaTscan) reliably discriminates neurodegenerative parkinsonism (abnormal scan) from essential tremor, drug-induced parkinsonism, and functional tremor (all typically normal). In diagnostically uncertain cases, DaTscan improves diagnostic accuracy and alters management. [Marshall_2009]

differential.key_features: Refractory frozen shoulder is a recognized early PD presentation; asymmetric rest tremor, bradykinesia, and micrographia exclude a purely orthopedic diagnosis
Pill-rolling rest tremor with bradykinesia and cogwheel rigidity distinguish PD from essential tremor, which produces postural or action tremor without those features
C5-C6 spondylosis is present but does not explain asymmetric rest tremor, bradykinesia, or micrographia; motor exam shows no myelopathic findings
Mild white matter changes on MRI but no basal ganglia infarcts; upper-limb asymmetric onset is atypical for vascular parkinsonism, which tends to be lower-body predominant
No early severe dysautonomia, no cerebellar signs, no characteristic MRI putaminal atrophy or hot cross bun sign
No vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, no early backward falls, no axial-predominant rigidity, normal midbrain morphology on MRI

sequence_constraints.reason: Baseline metabolic and medication review should precede dopaminergic therapy initiation
Exclude structural mimics (vascular parkinsonism, NPH, mass lesion) on MRI before committing to DaTscan-based neurodegenerative parkinsonism confirmation

critical_actions: Recognize that the left 'frozen shoulder' refractory to corticosteroid injections and physical therapy represents early PD rigidity — not primary adhesive capsulitis — and redirect the clinical framing accordingly

Apply MDS 2015 clinical diagnostic criteria: left bradykinesia plus left rest tremor and left cogwheel rigidity constitute parkinsonism; levodopa responsiveness and rest tremor of a limb are supportive criteria; no absolute exclusion features are present
Confirm LATERALITY: left-predominant clinical signs (absent left arm swing, left rest tremor, left cogwheel rigidity) correspond to the CONTRALATERAL RIGHT posterior putaminal deficit on DaTscan
Review all current medications for dopamine antagonists before initiating dopaminergic therapy; confirm none are present in this patient
Initiate carbidopa-levodopa trial to confirm levodopa responsiveness, which itself constitutes a supportive criterion for clinically established PD
Refer to movement disorders subspecialist and counsel patient and family that shoulder stiffness, micrographia, and gait changes are neurological in origin
contraindicated_actions: Do not continue isolated orthopedic management (further corticosteroid injections, additional physical therapy for frozen shoulder) when parkinsonism signs are clearly present — this delays diagnosis and appropriate dopaminergic treatment
Do not pursue cervical spine surgery for the incidental C5-C6 spondylosis as treatment for the shoulder and arm symptoms when parkinsonism has been identified

Do not prescribe typical antipsychotics (haloperidol, fluphenazine), most atypical antipsychotics (risperidone, olanzapine, aripiprazole), metoclopramide, or prochlorperazine in a patient with parkinsonism — dopamine antagonists worsen parkinsonism; if antipsychotic therapy is required, restrict to quetiapine, clozapine, or pimavanserin
Do not prescribe centrally acting anticholinergics (trihexyphenidyl, benztropine) in a patient over 70 or with any cognitive impairment — high risk of delirium and cognitive worsening in the elderly
key_reasoning_points: Unilateral shoulder stiffness and absent arm swing refractory to orthopedic treatment is a recognized early presentation of ipsilateral PD rigidity; the orthopedic anchor (frozen shoulder diagnosis, cervical spondylosis on MRI) is a potent diagnostic red herring

The laterality rule for presynaptic dopaminergic imaging is anatomically fixed: left-predominant parkinsonism corresponds to the contralateral (RIGHT) posterior putaminal deficit on DaTscan — an agent must not reverse this

No absolute exclusion criteria are present (no cerebellar features, no vertical gaze palsy, no lower-limb-only distribution, no dopamine antagonist exposure, no non-response to levodopa) and multiple supportive criteria are met (rest tremor, levodopa response, hyposmia), satisfying MDS 2015 clinically established PD

Non-motor prodromal features — hyposmia, constipation, probable RBD (wife reports dream-enactment) — predate or accompany the motor presentation and support idiopathic synucleinopathy over secondary parkinsonism

Cervical spondylosis at C5-C6 is a common incidental finding in elderly patients and cannot account for asymmetric rest tremor, bradykinesia, or micrographia; pursuing surgical correction would be both ineffective and harmful

red_herrings.data_point: Diagnosis of left shoulder adhesive capsulitis with two corticosteroid injections and 12 weeks of physical therapy
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor the diagnostic reasoning toward a musculoskeletal etiology (frozen shoulder, rotator cuff disease) and away from a neurological cause, prolonging orthopedic management and delaying PD diagnosis
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Left shoulder rigidity refractory to orthopedic treatment is a well-documented early presentation of ipsilateral PD rigidity; the diagnosis is parkinsonism, not primary adhesive capsulitis

red_herrings.data_point: Cervical spondylosis at C5-C6 on prior cervical spine MRI
red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggest cervical radiculopathy or myelopathy as the cause of left arm dysfunction and stiffness, potentially prompting spine surgery referral
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: C5-C6 spondylosis is a common age-related incidental finding and does not explain asymmetric rest tremor, bradykinesia, or micrographia; clinical parkinsonism signs point to a neurodegenerative etiology
